cells.tense: The work sits steady under your hands at the bench right now.
cells.ask: When one stretch finishes, name what it was for, then leave it alone for a day.
cells.core:
You sit down and the passes come, each one finding what the last one missed. Strangers think this kind of progress takes grinding. You've learned it takes adjusting a little at a time until the shape comes right — and the calm to keep at it shows in the surface of the thing. Someone looking at the finished piece sees a person who wasn't in a hurry.

The pull to keep refining is working for you rather than against you. Nothing here needs to be pried loose. The one cost is that this balance goes quiet when a piece ends and your hands sit empty, which is where the loosening usually happens. So when something is done, hand it on with its reason attached, and let the next one wait its turn.

cells.tense: There's a finished version somewhere ahead, and you're pressing on toward it.
cells.ask: Show one unfinished piece to another person this week, on purpose.
cells.core:
Every piece that comes off your hands reads as a draft of the version that's still ahead, so none of them get to be done. You're not showing off for a crowd — you're running the passes early, chasing the point where it's finally deep enough, and the ease that made the work good is the fee you're paying for it.

You started this because something in it was true, and it doesn't stop being yours just because you set it down for a night. So show one unfinished piece to someone. Not to fix it and not for praise, just to let the light in and watch what holds. Whatever you notice stays with you; the work is still yours.
cells.sheetLine: The work isn't keeping you from the future. Wanting it is.

cells.tense: You say the work isn't ready to be seen, and the bench has been cold a while.
cells.ask: Take one honest look at what you have, and say in one plain sentence what it's for and who it serves.
cells.core:
There's a way this goes when it's working: a piece gets finished, it goes out, someone uses it, and the next pass starts from what you learned. That loop is what keeps a craft alive. The loop here is broken at one place — the part where the work leaves your hands — and no amount of skill at the bench repairs that from the inside.

You've been telling people it isn't ready yet, and the bench has gone cold in the meantime. The showing has stopped. What's missing is your own say-so: one plain sentence about what you've made and what it serves. Say it out loud for your own ears first, so the work has a direction before anyone else weighs in.

cells.tense: This craft is already running deeper than you admit, and you call it staying busy.
cells.ask: Write one line about what you did at the bench today, and add what it changed for someone.
cells.core:
You reach for particular tools in a particular order, you know which flaw you're working out this month — there's a craft with a shape here, and it gets described as though it were something that happens to you. The skill is real. The one doing it isn't claimed.

The line isn't mastery. It's whether a person says out loud that they're at the bench on purpose, and builds from there. So write one line: what you did today, and what it changed for someone. That's not a plan or a promise, just a line you keep, and keeping it makes the work yours to name.
cells.sheetLine: You're already building this. You just call it staying busy.

attempts.check: The record says the skill at the bench is reaching a real threshold; it does not say who the practice is for, how long it has run, or whether the early room went badly, and my drafts must not supply those. A reader who has been at this work for years and is happy with a quiet, private practice would rightly say I have read a season as a wound — so each cell has to describe what the person could watch themselves doing this afternoon rather than why they got here. The asks stay useful even if I am wrong about the status: finishing and noticing a stretch of real work, making something in reach of other people, saying what the standard is, writing down what went right are all worth doing regardless. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of the artisan-becoming-master line — it sounds wise and tells the person nothing they could check.
